disease_info: Delusional Disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more persistent delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thought, or marked negative symptoms seen in schizophrenia. Outside of the impact of the delusional beliefs, functioning is often relatively preserved, and behavior may not appear obviously odd or bizarre to casual observers. The content of the delusions is typically non‑bizarre or only mildly implausible (e.g., being conspired against, deceived by a partner, or having a hidden illness), and mood symptoms, if present, are usually secondary and not pervasive. It is distinguished from psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia by the lack of significant cognitive disorganization and from mood disorders with psychotic features by the independence of the delusions from mood episodes, with a course that can be chronic and insidiously progressive.

narrative.stressor: About two years ago, Lissette’s husband underwent surgery for worsening cardiac problems, which shifted much of the household management and caregiving onto her just as she was beginning to feel her own age‑related health worries. Around this time, she became increasingly preoccupied with the idea that certain neighbors and even clinic staff were quietly interfering with her husband’s care and monitoring her activities through community events she coordinated. Over the following 1 year and 9 months, she gradually withdrew from some festival planning and book‑club meetings, insisting on handling medical appointments alone and double‑checking every interaction in ways that strained long‑standing friendships at the Honduran community center. Her adult daughter finally persuaded her to see a psychiatrist after Lissette refused home‑health services she believed were part of the interference and her suspicions began to disrupt both her caregiving and the couple’s usual involvement in church and cultural gatherings.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I know people around my husband’s doctors are secretly working against us, and no one can convince me otherwise.”

narrative.stressor: As Tyler began competing for more prestigious composing commissions and a potential regional symphony leadership role, he faced a series of rejections and lukewarm feedback that sharply contrasted with his meticulous preparation. Shortly after a major grant proposal was turned down nearly two years ago, he became convinced that a small group of colleagues and a former professor were secretly coordinating to block his career, interpreting routine scheduling changes and neutral emails as part of a deliberate effort to undermine him. Over the next 1 year and 9 months, this belief hardened despite reassurances, leading him to confront administrators, decline collaborative projects, and spend late nights combing through past reviews and social media for “evidence,” which alarmed his spouse and bandmates as his professional relationships deteriorated. He was finally brought to psychiatric evaluation after he threatened to withdraw from a coveted residency he had actually been awarded, insisting it was a trap designed by the same people he believed had been sabotaging his work.
narrative.chief_complaint: “For almost two years I’ve been certain certain people in the music scene are secretly coordinating to destroy my career, and nothing anyone says changes that.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly two years ago, after a period of increased travel and late nights related to a store remodel, Cassidy and her spouse had several tense arguments about time together and social boundaries. Around this time, Cassidy began to focus intensely on small, ordinary behaviors—her spouse checking their phone, changing passwords, or being quiet after work—as signs of a hidden agenda, gradually building a fixed narrative that her partner and even some friends were secretly exchanging information about her and testing her loyalty. Over the ensuing 1 year and 9 months, she remained high‑energy at work but grew more suspicious in her marriage, insisting on interpreting casual comments and social media posts as coded messages, which led to repeated conflicts about trust and privacy despite the absence of any confirming evidence. Her spouse eventually suggested counseling, and when couples therapy stalled because Cassidy could not let go of these ideas, the therapist recommended an individual psychiatric evaluation to better understand the fixed beliefs that were driving the relationship strain.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t shake the belief that my spouse and friends have been secretly plotting behind my back, no matter how much they deny it.”
